messages.subject: Road-based distance sampling transects
parts:
Hi all,

I am a PhD student using distance sampling for the first time. I used somewhat unorthodox methods and am hoping for some advice on two quick questions about the best course of action for analysis. 

1.  I drove road transects, recording the position of all animals sighted on a map of high-resolution satellite imagery (rather than recording distance and angle to animal). I am aware that this violates some of the typical assumptions of distance sampling. Are there any methods I can use to estimate density that are robust to this approach?
2. Using a laser rangefinder, I estimated the visibility on both sides of the road, every 500 m. Given that my transects are longer than 500 m, I have multiple such measurements per transect. Is there an appropriate way for me to incorporate these visibility measurements into the probability function I will use, given that the visibility taken each 500 m does not precisely represent the visibility at all points along the transect?

Any information would be much appreciated!

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Road-based distance sampling transects
parts:
Henry

Welcome to the list. As you note, surveys restricted to roads induce bias in your estimates. There are two reasons for this. First, roads are not placed randomly on the landscape, hence they do not provide a representative sample of your study area. If you only want to make inference to the region on either side of the roads, inference to this region might be valid. 

Second, your study animal knows about the presence of the road—they are either attracted or repulsed by the presence of the road and associated traffic. In either case, animals are not distributed uniformly at all distances from the road. In this situation, you will need data not only to estimate the shape of the detection function as a function of distance from the road, but you will also need to estimate the shape of the animal availability gradient. Estimating these two functions requires the collection of additional data and cannot be done retrospectively.  Papers below discuss this:

  • Marques, T. A., Buckland, S. T., Bispo, R., & Howland, B. (2013). Accounting for animal density gradients using independent information in distance sampling surveys. Statistical Methods and Applications, 22, 67–80. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10260-012-0223-2
  • Marques, T. A., Buckland, S. T., Borchers, D. L., Tosh, D., & McDonald, R. A. (2010). Point transect sampling along linear features. Biometrics, 66, 1247–1255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x
  • Borchers, D.L. and Cox, M.J. (2017), Distance sampling detection functions: 2D or not 2D?. Biom, 73: 593-602. https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.12581
Your rangefinder data on visibility will not provide information about animal availability which central to resolving your situation.
